extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists (students and professionals) seeking practical guidance on writing mathematics, proofs, algorithms, and related documentation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writing mathematics and CS texts (papers, manuals, documentation), drawn from Don Knuth et al.'s Stanford course; focuses on notation, presentation, documentation, figures/tables, and the publication/refereeing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete before-and-after examples
rubrics_metrics.description: We saw many examples of ``before'' and ``after'' from manuscripts in progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete before/after manuscript excerpts to illustrate how revisions improve clarity, notation, structure, and exposition. Demonstrations of edits help teach practical rewriting techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive subscripts and superscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: We learned how to avoid excessive subscripts and superscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler, clearer notation; minimize stacked indices and complicated superscripting that impede readability. Rework notation to reduce visual clutter and cognitive load for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document algorithms, programs, and user manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: We discussed the documentation of algorithms, computer programs, and user manuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat documentation as an integral part of mathematical/CS writing: explain the purpose, inputs/outputs, usage, and behavior of algorithms and programs; provide clear instructions in user manuals and comments so others can understand and reuse the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the refereeing and editing process
rubrics_metrics.description: We considered the process of refereeing and editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with referees and editors in mind: present claims clearly, supply necessary evidence, anticipate likely questions, and make it easy for reviewers to verify results. Learn typical editorial expectations and common reasons for rejection or revision requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make effective diagrams and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: We studied how to make effective diagrams and tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design figures and tables to convey information efficiently: choose clear labels, appropriate scales, and readable layout. Use visuals to complement and clarify the text rather than clutter it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate quotations to enhance the text
rubrics_metrics.description: and how to find appropriate quotations to spice up a text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select quotations that illuminate, motivate, or humanize the material; use them sparingly and ensure they are relevant and correctly attributed so they enhance rather than distract from the technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address mathematics- and computer-science-specific writing issues
rubrics_metrics.description: the vast majority of the lectures were devoted to issues that are specific to mathematics and/or computer science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to genre-specific concerns (e.g., theorem/proof structure, formal definitions, pseudocode conventions, complexity discussion) that differ from general English writing classes; adapt exposition to the conventions and expectations of math/CS readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errata reporting procedure and communication conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Please send suggested corrections to knuth-bug@cs.stanford.edu, or send snail mail to Prof. D. Knuth... He may not be able to read your message until many months have gone by... DO NOT SEND EMAIL TO KNUTH-BUG EXCEPT TO REPORT ERRORS IN BOOKS! And if you do report an error via email, please do not include attachments of any kind; your message should be readable on brand-X operating systems for all values of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting errors: use the specified email or postal address, restrict messages to error reports only, avoid attachments, and send plain-text readable messages to maximize cross-platform accessibility. Expect delayed replies.
